books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

stimulus.text: Margaret Fuller, a member of Emerson's circle in Concord, published Woman in the Nineteenth Century in 1845. She argued that women, like men, should be free to develop their minds and characters, and she edited the transcendentalist journal The Dial. The photograph shows Fuller in 1846, seated in profile, reading a book on a stand with her hand raised to her forehead.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the lesson script on transcendentalism: Emerson's circle included Margaret Fuller, whose 1845 Woman in the Nineteenth Century fed the Seneca Falls generation. Photograph: daguerreotype of Margaret Fuller by John Plumbe, Jr., 1846 (National Portrait Gallery). Public domain; image viewed before writing. Description records only what the photograph visibly shows.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Fuller's book best shows that transcendentalist ideas about the individual did which of the following?

options.text: Applied only to men in Concord
options.misconception: The circle met in Concord among men, so it is easy to think its ideas stopped there.

options.text: Were rejected by every reformer of the 1840s
options.misconception: Transcendentalists kept their distance from reform groups, so it is easy to think reformers rejected them.

options.text: Extended to argue for women's equality and self-development
Had nothing to do with reform movements
options.misconception: Thoreau and Emerson criticized reform groups, so it is easy to cut transcendentalism off from reform.

rationales.A: Fuller herself was in the circle, and her book applies self-trust to women directly.
rationales.B: Fuller's book fed the Seneca Falls generation; reformers took the ideas up, they did not reject them.
rationales.C: If each person carries something divine within, then women too may develop mind and character freely.
rationales.D: The same confidence in the individual powered temperance, abolition, and women's rights.
rationales.general:
1. Take Emerson's idea and change the subject. Self-trust for every person — then ask who 'every person' leaves out.
2. Watch Fuller close the gap. She argues women, like men, should develop their minds and characters.
Background: Fuller's 1845 book fed the generation that met at Seneca Falls in 1848.
Remember: a big idea is tested by asking who it leaves out — and who picks it up to include them.
